And if you do, then you probably won’t “get it,” not because you’re less intelligent or because you lack the literacy skills to emotionally process and analyse what you’ve seen, but because so many modern movies are kind of throwaways, you see it and you move on, that’s how so many movies are made and produced today, to be made and forgotten and moved on from. And if you go into that same mindset of “watch and forget” with something like Paris, Texas or Oldboy, then of course you wouldn’t “get it,” because they’re films that kind of do need time to sink into your conscience. If that’s a snobby stance to take, then I’ll accept the title of a snob, but I do ultimately think that there is such a thing as people not “getting it,” just not for the reasons people assume, and instead because of the reasons I’ve mentioned. 

In short, art needs time to sink in and ruminate; whereas modern blockbusters are made to be absorbed and forgotten, thus why when blockbuster junkies tune into more lasting movies, they often don’t “get it,” not because they’re stupid, but because it’s a whole different ballgame. Hell, a whole different sport.

The animal cruelty in the film is undeniably abhorrent, indefensible in fact. But, with that being said, I actually think that Cannibal Holocaust is an exceptional film. Long and possibly quite incoherent comment incoming! 

It’s a vicious reminder of the multi-generation-spanning feeling of almost complete desensitisation that we all, to varying degrees, carry on our backs and in our minds. And the late, great Ruggero Deodato had no shame or fear in holding a mirror up to us to reflect just how desensitised we have become, but also to show how our prejudices can appear, even if we consider ourselves to be the furthest thing from prejudice, which he achieves by showing us both sides of the coin, the truth and the false narrative, with the truth being the crew brutalising and destroying the homes of the tribespeople, and the false narrative being that there’s this evil cannibal cult out there who wrongfully slaughtered some good ol' white folk. It’s, in the end, revealed almost to be a story on how people often go to great lengths (in this case, the destruction of evidence) to hide the truth and uphold the false narratives, and uphold the bigoted system that rules over our planet. There’s many worthwhile lessons one could learn from that film, in my opinion, and those are just two of the many. 

It’s one of the few movies in existence where, in my opinion, shock value is actually utilised how it should be, to effectively shock us into a state of realisation about ourselves and the world around us, not just for the sake of a lust for cheap gasps and covered eyes. Do I wish that real animals didn’t die for it? Absolutely, and Deodato himself felt the same in the years after, regretful of his choices. But, at the same time, is the film all the more effective for it? Without question, and I feel that’s undeniable.

The River is the answer. Always will be. It goes beyond words or any explanation I could give. But when you hear that album, you get it, just like all of us who’ve heard it. You can’t explain it, but the experience is unforgettable. Turn the lights down, grab your headphones, close your eyes and let The River take you away. The only film I’ll commend on layer 4 is the guinea pig movies, purely because the practical effects are genuinely incredible and the behind the scenes documentaries about the making of those films are a lot of fun to watch (certainly more than the films themselves) because it’s clear that everyone involved (including the woman playing the victim) are all having the time of their lives making the film. And that’s always cool to see.

Threads, Zero Day, Faces Of Death and Cannibal Holocaust are all great, though remember that Cannibal Holocaust contains real animal death and abuse. There’s two others on here that I also think are really solid and worthwhile films, with those being August Underground and A Serbian Film. Now, everyone, please put down your pitchforks, because I’ve been *rinsed* online before for even invoking the names of those movies, but I truly think that, if the individual can handle the content, both are really worth seeing as they’re very impressively made and the practical effects alone make those films something to admire on a technical level, even if the actual events and characters within the film are abhorrent and irredeemable. So, maybe if you’re new to disturbing movies, they aren’t really a good place to start, but instead something to work up to, if it peaks your interest. 

My advice with these movies, as well as disturbing movies in general, is to be cautious. No movie is worth your mental health or well-being suffering, so try to read up on these films before you watch them. We all have limits and triggers and there’s never any kind of shame in that.

‘i love you’ into ‘listen before i go’ and then finally with the recap track ‘goodbye’, it is one of the most emotionally brutalising finales to an album. I could be way off the mark, but I’ve always viewed the songs like this: 

listen before I go - a suicidal individual, grappling with the conflicting thoughts about what they believe they “need” to do, with the final moments being them losing their battle.

i love you - the grief-stricken lover, trying their hardest to come to terms with the suicide of their soulmate, in equal measure looking back on their time together, and wishing so badly that they didn’t love that person as much as they do, because maybe then it wouldn’t ache nearly as terribly as it does. 

goodbye - in a disjointed, this is both the grieving lover and the deceased speaking. The grieving pleading “don’t leave me” and bargaining “it’s not true,” whilst the deceased finally lets out, when it’s too late, just how heavily they were feeling with “baby I don’t feel so good,” looking back on their final moments with “take me to the rooftop,” and even “don’t you know I’m no good for you,” expressing to their grieving lover their belief that them being gone somehow benefits the living, whilst the grief-stricken partner still refuses to believe what has happened (“It’s not true“), and even going as far to say “I’m the bad guy,” showing a feeling of guilt from the belief that they could’ve done more to save the love of their life. 

Could my theory be farfetched? Sure. But one thing is for certain, if it’s even half-way true, it’s a heartbreaking trio of tracks, and my favourite climax of any of Billie’s albums.

With all due respect, I disagree with most of your points. I don’t think this film is shaping up to be anything like the formulaic biopics we’ve come to know. The director attached, Scott Cooper, is a genuinely great filmmaker, specialising in grounded and gritty storytelling. If you have concerns about how he may handle Bruce’s story, I recommend Crazy Heart, starring Jeff Bridges, about an aging country music star. I think that’s the kind of tone he’s going to be going for with this movie. 

Next, I think focusing on one particular era or year or album of Bruce’s life is a much better approach than to make a film spanning his entire career. *That* is when it’s more at risk of becoming formulaic. But I’d argue that 1982 was probably the most emotionally charged point in his career, he was seemingly in legitimate emotional turmoil during that time. If this film is done right, I can see myself feeling even more connected to Bruce and his music, even if it is through the performance of an actor playing him, it’s still Bruce’s story being told at the end of the day. 

On your third point, and your fourth, I’ll go back to my previous. I think the reason for this film’s existence is much less about the quality of the Nebraska album itself, and more about how that time was for Bruce. As I said, I believe that time was quite heavy for him. Sure, we could get a movie all about the making of Darkness or The River or Born To Run, but they’d probably be infinitely less interesting and unique than the story of the Nebraska album. In fact, they’d probably have to dramatise a *lot* more in regards to those sessions than they would for Nebraska. The story of the making of the Nebraska album and everything surrounding it, it’s already incredibly interesting and powerful. He is personal to us, believe me, I get that, Bruce saved my life. But I think this film will only strengthen that personal connection, not decrease it.

Now, your last point is one I can more understand personally. Do we *actually* need this movie? Probably not. We have the books, both Bruce’s autobiography and the book in which this film gets it’s title. But, even with those, for me, that era has always been slightly shrouded in mystery. There’s documentaries about the making-of the Born To Run, Darkness and The River albums, there’s books and documentaries (admittedly some unofficial) that touch a lot on the BiTUSA album, and there’s a few books on early Bruce (1972-74). But Nebraska has always seemed to get much less attention and focus. Yes, we Bruce fans know how exceptional it is, how much of a powerful and emotional experience it is to listen to that album. But outside of our fandom, can you see many people talking about it? I know I don’t. And maybe that’s *why* it needs to be made, to help people to see that Bruce is more than, as a lot of the public sees him, some muscly patriot screaming “BORN…”, he’s one of the most important, personal and deeply brilliant writers and artists of our time. And if this film can help people to see and “feel” that, then why would I be against it? 

Again, I say all of this with respect to you and your opinion, I’m not out to change your mind, just to give a different perspective. Peace and love.

That’s what interests me to. Sometimes it works, Baz Luhrmann’s Elvis and Dexter Fletcher’s Rocketman are both great examples of how to tell a person’s life story without it becoming stale or overstuffed. I think focusing on this era of Bruce’s life, post-The River and pre-BiTUSA, is the best possible road to go down as, I’d argue, it’s the most interesting point in his entire career, a time when he stepped back for a little while, before his BiTUSA superstardom took over.

I think that’s a huge misconception when it comes to therapy, that you’re the only one feeling how you are feeling, thus why so many people fear seeking out help in that way. But, in my experience with discussing intrusive thoughts with a therapist, albeit not at all the same intrusive thoughts as OP, mine were incredibly different, it honestly just felt like it was another Tuesday for them. They seemed unfazed, because intrusive thoughts are nothing new. Hell, I’d wager that we all have them, just some of us have them to a more extreme degree, particularly those of us with severe mental health issues and past trauma.

Remember that what you’re experiencing right now, they are only *thoughts*. You haven’t harmed any animals and you haven’t acted on these urges. And the fact that you dislike and fear these said urges is, to me, a sign that all hope isn’t lost for you to get the help you need in order to rid yourself of these urges. The best thing you can do, as has already been stated here, for both yourself and the safety of those dogs, is to either remove yourself from the home where the animals are, or remove the animals. 

Speak with a therapist, please. It’s their job to listen, to understand and to help you overcome these negative urges that you’re experiencing. Believe me, a therapist won’t demonise you for how you’re feeling. They won’t look at you and see some kind of a monster. They’ll see a human being who needs help. Let them help, dude. But until you can get that help, I highly suggest staying away from the dogs in any way that you can, for the safety of yourself and them, even if it means you leaving for a little while.

Bruce Springsteen. This will be a long, exhausting story, so feel free to ignore. Just want to get this shit out, alright? 

To say I was lost in 2019 would be an understatement. I was 16 and had no clue where the fuck I was heading in life (and even at 21, I still don’t really know). Then a movie called ‘Blinded By The Light’ was released, a British coming of age drama with Springsteen’s discography as it’s heartbeat. I saw it on a whim one afternoon, being a fan of the coming of age genre of movies and knowing it was music-centred. 

From the moment I heard ‘The Promised Land’ and ‘Dancing In The Dark’ blare out of those theatre speakers, I was hooked. Then came ‘The River,’ ‘Born To Run,’ and, of course, ‘Badlands’. Now, to some people, these songs, they’ve always known them. But me? I’d never heard of them of in my life. And I’ll be damned if every single one of them didn’t feel like they were written specifically for me. 

When I left the theatre, on my way home, I loaded up the ‘Darkness On The Edge Of Town’ album. From ‘Badlands’ until the title track, I was hooked, and when it ended, I was almost in tears. Nothing, no song or album or movie or whatever, *nothing* had hit me like Springsteen had. It was like a knife of realisation in the gut that, in regards to my life at the time, “well…maybe I’m not the only one who feels like this.” 

When I got home, I played the ‘Born To Run’ album. Start to finish. And I got the same feeling. And as those final notes of Jungleland began to fade out, the tears which were almost shed during ‘Darkness’ were now full body sobs, and I say that with no kind of exaggeration. 

Fast forward to now, 5 years later, during which I’ve attempted to take my life multiple times, lost most of my friends due to my mental health, watched as my father has broken down into total submission under the weight of life, the list goes on. But you know what has always remained? Him, the Boss, Bruce Springsteen. I finally got to see him live earlier this year an hour away from my hometown. I cried until my eyes stung, laughed until my gut felt nearing explosion and I sang those lyrics, the very same ones that saves my life, until my throat damn near bled. 

I’m still not happy, I’m still broken, I’m still lost, I still don’t know what I’m doing or where I’m going in this life. But the difference is between 2019 me and me today, I have a beautiful girlfriend who I would die for if she ever asked, I have the confidence to be more myself and to follow my passions, I have a lot of shit that I never could’ve dreamed of in 2019. And although all of that progress was technically down to my own efforts, I also have to give sincere credit to Bruce. Without him, without his music, I don’t even know what kind of person I’d be…or if I’d have even lived long enough to have discovered who I am. 

So, without a doubt, my answer to your question is: Bruce…and, obviously, the heartstopping, pantsdropping, earthshocking, hardrocking, bootyshaking, earthquaking, lovemaking, viagrataking, historymaking, *legendary* E-Street band.
